last_material_result: One bounded pain-led discovery round tested a Seoul stroller/wheelchair subway transfer-route utility and rejected the cluster before allocating an MB item ID. The pain is clearly real: published field research found accessible transfers at some Seoul interchange stations can take 18-20 minutes versus 2-3 minutes for non-wheelchair riders. However, the substitute landscape is already unusually strong. Muui has published accessibility transfer maps covering roughly 80 interchange stations, KakaoMap exposes Seoul Metro accessibility-route/platform gap information, and Seoul's own Seoul Donghaeng Map was launched specifically to provide mobility-impaired users including wheelchair and stroller users with accessible routing, elevator/facility information and integrated transport support. Three plausible wedges were considered — stroller-specific transfer time, elevator-only interchange routing, and station accessibility risk scoring — but each is either directly covered by incumbents or would require ongoing facility/outage normalization to remain trustworthy. This is therefore a poor low-maintenance independent B2C wedge despite genuine pain.
economics: KRW0 spent. Consumer pain is strong but acquisition and differentiation are weak because official and specialized free substitutes already cover accessible routing and station-level guidance. A credible independent version would inherit freshness/safety maintenance without a correspondingly strong monetization edge, so expected contribution does not justify build burden.
next_checkpoint: Next iteration run a fresh genetic discovery round outside parking, concert-return, bulky-waste fee and accessibility-routing clusters. Prefer a local consumer action where official data exists but official products stop at raw lookup rather than already solving the end decision.
recommendation: REJECT the Seoul stroller/wheelchair subway routing cluster before candidate promotion; allocate no MB ID. Continue DISCOVER next iteration.
